power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

live_data_statements: Most participants were enrolled following motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) and were Black, female, socioeconomically disadvantaged, with high levels of peritraumatic distress (Ext.
Participants were classified according to recovery across the 10 APNS (Ext.

Participants were drawn from the AURORA Study, a longitudinal observational multisite cohort study designed to investigate pain and neuropsychiatric recovery following traumatic stress exposure (TSE) 1 .
Between September 2017 and July 2020, n=2,626 individuals were enrolled from 33 Emergency Departments (ED)s across the United States within 72 hours of a TSE.

Participants were eligible if they had no major physical injuries (e.g., no solid organ injury Grade >1 based on the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma criteria, no significant hemorrhage, no need for a chest tube or operation with general anesthesia), were alert and oriented, fluent in English, between the ages of 18-75, and unlikely to be admitted to the hospital for >72 hours.

Enrolled participants completed questionnaires and provided blood samples in the ED and were followed longitudinally for 12 months with repeated pain and neuropsychiatric assessments over that time and blood collection at two followup timepoints (2 weeks (2WK) and 6 months (6M)).
All participants provided written informed consent under protocols approved by the institutional review boards of each participating site.

For the present analysis, trajectory classes comprising fewer than 20 participants were merged with the most phenotypically similar class within the same APNS, based on changes in symptom severity from the ED to 6 months) (calculated as Ed minus 6M symptom scores).

Libraries were multiplexed in batches of 96, with all longitudinal samples from each participant assigned to the same sequencing batch to minimize batchrelated variability in within-participant comparisons.
Because all longitudinal samples from a given participant were sequenced within the same batch, the paired design also minimized potential confounding from between-batch technical variation.
Participants assigned to Recovery trajectories in at least seven APNS and Chronic trajectories in fewer than two APNS were classified as "Most-Recovered" (n = 96).
Participants assigned to Chronic trajectories in at least two APNS and Recovery trajectories in fewer than seven APNS were classified as "Most-Chronic" (n = 82).
All remaining participants were classified as "Intermediate" (n = 67) and were excluded from model training and feature selection.
Intermediate participants were retained as an additional heldout group and were not included in model fitting or feature selection.
For each APNS, participants assigned to Chronic trajectories were compared with those assigned to all other trajectories using ROC analyses and AUC estimates.
Participants were stratified into high and low RRS groups using the median RRS value from the full cohort of 245 participants as the cutoff.

Participants were assigned to post-TSE symptom trajectories for each of ten adverse posttraumatic neuropsychiatric sequelae (APNS) using growth mixture modeling of longitudinal self-reported symptom severity (2-4 trajectories per APNS).
Participants were stratified into high and low RRS groups using a median split.

The thresholds used to define Most-Recovered (≥7 Recovery trajectories, <2 Chronic trajectories) and Most-Chronic (≥2 Chronic trajectories, <7 Recovered trajectories) groups are highlighted; remaining participants were classified as Intermediate. b.
